title: First-degree intentional homicide
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant caused the death of another human being with the intent to kill that person or another, without the presence of mitigating circumstances as defined in subsection (2).

title: Attempted first-degree intentional homicide
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant took substantial steps toward causing the death of another human being with the intent to kill that person or another, without the presence of mitigating circumstances as defined in subsection (2).

title: First-degree reckless homicide
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant recklessly caused the death of another human being and that the defendant’s actions were under circumstances demonstrating utter disregard for human life.

title: First-degree reckless homicide (“Len Bias law”)
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant caused the death of another human being by either manufacturing, distributing, delivering, or administering certain controlled substances in violation of s. 961.41, and that the use of such substances resulted in the death of the individual.

title: Felony murder - underlying crime completed
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant caused the death of another human being while committing or attempting to commit one of the specified felonies.
elements: While Committing or Attempting to Commit a Specified Felony

title: Second-degree intentional homicide
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant caused the death of another human being with intent to kill that person or another.

title: Second-degree reckless homicide
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant recklessly caused the death of another human being.

title: Homicide by negligent handling of a dangerous weapon, explosives, or fire
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant caused the death of another human being by negligently operating or handling a dangerous weapon, explosives, or fire.
elements: Involvement of a Dangerous Weapon, Explosives, or Fire

title: Homicide by operation of a vehicle while under the influence
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant caused the death of another human being by operating or handling a vehicle while under the influence of an intoxicant.
elements: Operation or Handling of a Vehicle
Under the Influence of an Intoxicant

title: Homicide by operation of a vehicle while the person has a detectable amount of a restricted controlled substance
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant caused the death of another human being by operating or handling a vehicle while having a detectable amount of a restricted controlled substance in their blood.
elements: Operation or Handling of a Vehicle
Detectable Amount of a Restricted Controlled Substance

title: Homicide by operation of a vehicle with a prohibited alcohol concentration
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant caused the death of another human being by operating or handling a vehicle while having a prohibited alcohol concentration, as defined in s. 340.01(46m).
elements: Operation or Handling of a Vehicle

title: Homicide by operation or handling of a firearm or airgun while under the influence
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant caused the death of another human being by operating or handling a firearm or airgun while under the influence of an intoxicant.
elements: Operation or Handling of a Firearm or Airgun
Under the Influence of an Intoxicant

title: Homicide by operation or handling of a firearm or airgun with an alcohol concentration of 0.08 or More
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant caused the death of another human being by operating or handling a firearm or airgun while having an alcohol concentration of 0.08 or more.
elements: Operation or Handling of a Firearm or Airgun

title: Homicide by negligent operation of a vehicle
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant caused the death of another human being through the negligent operation or handling of a vehicle.
elements: Negligent Operation or Handling of a Vehicle

title: Mutilating a corpse
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant mutilated, disfigured, or dismembered a corpse with the intent to conceal a crime or avoid apprehension, prosecution, or conviction for a crime.

title: Hiding or burying a corpse
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant hid or buried a corpse with the intent to conceal a crime, avoid apprehension, prosecution, or conviction, or with the intent to collect benefits under certain public assistance programs.

title: Assisting Suicide
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant, with the intent that another person takes their own life, assisted that person in committing suicide.

title: Simple battery
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant caused bodily harm to another person with the intent to cause such harm, and that the act was done without the consent of the victim.

title: Substantial Battery: intent to cause bodily harm
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant caused substantial bodily harm to another person with the intent to cause bodily harm to that person or another.

title: Aggravated battery: intent to cause bodily harm
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant caused great bodily harm to another person with the intent to cause bodily harm to that person or another.

title: Aggravated battery: intent to cause great bodily harm
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant caused great bodily harm to another person with the intent to cause great bodily harm to that person or another.

title: Battery with substantial risk of great bodily harm
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant intentionally caused bodily harm to another person through conduct that created a substantial risk of great bodily harm. If the person harmed has a discernible or known physical disability, a rebuttable presumption arises that the conduct created a substantial risk of great bodily harm.
elements: Substantial Risk of Great Bodily Harm

title: Battery by prisoner
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant, a prisoner confined in a state prison or other detention facility, intentionally caused bodily harm or a soft tissue injury to an officer, employee, visitor, or another inmate without that person’s consent.
elements: Causing Bodily Harm or Soft Tissue Injury

title: Battery by certain committed persons
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant, a person detained or committed under specific civil commitment statutes, intentionally caused bodily harm to an officer, employee, agent, visitor, or another resident of the facility, without that person's consent.

title: Battery by a person subject to an injunction
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant, while subject to an injunction under specific statutes, intentionally caused bodily harm to the petitioner who sought the injunction, without the petitioner’s consent.

title: Battery to firefighter or commission warden
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant intentionally caused bodily harm to a firefighter or commission warden acting in an official capacity, with knowledge or reason to know the victim's role, and without the victim’s consent.

title: Battery or threat to a probation, extended supervision and parole agent, community supervision agent, or an aftercare agent
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant intentionally caused or threatened to cause bodily harm to a probation, extended supervision, or parole agent, a community supervision agent, an aftercare agent, or a family member of such an agent under specific circumstances.

title: Battery to a juror
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant intentionally caused bodily harm to a person because the victim served as a juror and participated in a verdict or indictment. The defendant must have known or had reason to know that the victim was a juror, and the harm must have been inflicted without the victim's consent.
elements: In Retaliation for a Verdict or Indictment

title: Battery to a public officer
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant intentionally caused bodily harm to a public officer either to influence the officer’s actions or as a result of an action taken by the officer in their official capacity. The bodily harm must have been inflicted without the officer’s consent.
elements: Victim’s Status as a Public Officer

title: Battery to a technical college district or school district officer or employee
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant intentionally caused bodily harm to a technical college district or school district officer or employee, knowing or having reason to know the victim’s status as such, and that the bodily harm was inflicted without the victim’s consent.

title: Battery to a public transit vehicle operator, driver or passenger
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant intentionally caused bodily harm to another person under specific circumstances involving public transit vehicles, such as while the victim is an operator, driver, or passenger, or in situations where the defendant forces the victim off or prevents access to a public transit vehicle.

title: Battery or threat to a witness
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant intentionally caused or threatened bodily harm to a person because they, or a family member or cohabitant, attended or testified as a witness.
elements: Victim’s Status as a Witness or Related Person

id: 940.203(2) — Battery or threat to a judge
title: Battery or threat to a judge
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant intentionally caused or threatened bodily harm to a judge or their family member under specific circumstances related to the official capacity of the judge.

id: 940.203(2) — Battery or threat to a prosecutor or law enforcement officer
title: Battery or threat to a prosecutor or law enforcement officer
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant intentionally caused or threatened bodily harm to a judge or their family member under specific circumstances related to the official capacity of the judge.

title: Battery or threat to a guardian ad litem, corporation counsel, advocate, or attorney
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant intentionally caused or threatened bodily harm to a current or former guardian ad litem, corporation counsel, advocate, attorney, or their family member in retaliation for actions taken in their official capacity.

title: Battery or threat to a staff member of a health care facility
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant intentionally caused or threatened bodily harm to a person who works or has worked in a health care facility, or to a family member of such a person, in retaliation for actions taken in a health care facility.
elements: Response to Health Care Facility Actions

title: Battery or threat to a health Care provider
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant intentionally caused or threatened bodily harm to a health care provider, or to a family member of a health care provider, in retaliation for actions taken by the health care provider in their professional capacity.
elements: Response to Health Care Provider’s Actions

title: Battery or threat to a Department of Revenue employee
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant intentionally caused or threatened bodily harm to a Department of Revenue official, employee, or agent, or their family member, in retaliation for actions taken in the official capacity of the official, employee, or agent.

title: Battery or threat to a Department of Safety and Professional Services or Department of Workforce Development Employee
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant intentionally caused or threatened bodily harm to a Department of Safety and Professional Services or Department of Workforce Development official, employee, or agent, or their family member, in retaliation for actions taken in the official capacity of the official, employee, or agent.

title: Battery to a county, city, village, or town employee
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant intentionally caused bodily harm to an employee of a county, city, village, or town who was enforcing or inspecting for compliance with construction-related laws or ordinances, and the defendant knew or should have known of the victim’s role.
elements: Victim’s Status as a Municipal Employee
Victim’s Role in Enforcement or Inspection

title: Mayhem
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant, with intent to disable or disfigure another person, intentionally cut or mutilated a part of the victim’s body.
elements: Cutting or Mutilating a Bodily Member

title: Sexual exploitation by therapist
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant, who is or holds themselves out to be a therapist, had sexual contact with a patient or client during an ongoing therapist-patient or therapist-client relationship.

title: First degree sexual assault: sexual contact or intercourse without consent causing great bodily harm or  pregnancy
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant had sexual contact or sexual intercourse with another person without their consent and caused pregnancy or great bodily harm to the victim as a result.
elements: Causing Pregnancy or Great Bodily Harm

title: First degree sexual assault: sexual contact or intercourse without consent by use or threat of a dangerous weapon
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant had sexual contact or sexual intercourse with another person without their consent and did so by using or threatening to use a dangerous weapon, or an article fashioned to make the victim reasonably believe it was a dangerous weapon.
elements: Use or Threat of a Dangerous Weapon

title: First degree sexual assault: sexual contact or intercourse without consent by use or threat of force or violence while aided and abetted
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant, while being aided or abetted by one or more other persons, had sexual contact or sexual intercourse with another person without their consent, and did so by using or threatening to use force or violence.
elements: Use or Threat of Force or Violence

title: Second degree sexual assault: sexual contact or intercourse without consent by use or threat of force or violence
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant had sexual contact or sexual intercourse with another person without their consent, and did so by using or threatening to use force or violence.
elements: Use or Threat of Force or Violence

title: Second degree sexual assault: sexual contact or intercourse without consent causing injury, illness, disease or impairment or a sexual or reproductive organ, or mental anguish requiring psychiatric care
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant had sexual contact or sexual intercourse with another person without their consent, and that the assault caused injury, illness, disease, or impairment of a sexual or reproductive organ, or caused mental anguish requiring psychiatric care for the victim.

title: Second degree sexual assault: sexual contact or intercourse with a person suffering from mental illness
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant had sexual contact or sexual intercourse with a person who suffers from a mental illness or deficiency that renders them incapable of appraising their own conduct, and that the defendant knew of this condition.

title: Second degree sexual assault: sexual contact or intercourse with a person who is under the influence of an intoxicant
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant had sexual contact or sexual intercourse with a person who was under the influence of an intoxicant to the extent that they were incapable of giving consent, and that the defendant had actual knowledge of this incapacity and the purpose of engaging in sexual activity while the victim was incapable of consenting.

title: Second degree sexual assault: sexual contact or intercourse with a person the defendant knows is unconscious
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant had sexual contact or sexual intercourse with a person who was unconscious, and that the defendant knew the person was unconscious at the time of the sexual activity.

title: Second degree sexual assault: sexual contact or intercourse without consent while aided and abetted
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant, while being aided or abetted by one or more other persons, had sexual contact or sexual intercourse with another person without that person’s consent.

title: Second degree sexual assault: sexual contact or intercourse without consent with a patient or resident
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant was an employee of a facility or program listed under s. 940.295(2)(b), (c), (h), or (k) and had sexual contact or sexual intercourse with a person who was a patient or resident of that facility or program.
elements: Victim’s Status as Patient or Resident

title: Second degree sexual assault: sexual contact or intercourse by a correctional staff member
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant, who is a correctional staff member, had sexual contact or sexual intercourse with an individual confined in a correctional institution.

title: Second degree sexual assault: sexual contact or intercourse by a probation, parole, or extended supervision agent
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant, who is a probation, parole, or extended supervision agent, had sexual contact or sexual intercourse with an individual under their supervision or influence.

title: Second degree sexual assault: sexual contact or intercourse by an employee of an entity
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant, who is a licensee, employee, or nonclient resident of a specified entity, had sexual contact or sexual intercourse with a client of that entity.

title: Second Degree Sexual Assault: Sexual Contact or Intercourse by a Law Enforcement Officer with a Person Detained or In Custody
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant, who is a law enforcement officer, had sexual contact or sexual intercourse with a person who was detained or in custody.
elements: Defendant’s Status as a Law Enforcement Officer

title: Third degree sexual assault: sexual intercourse without consent
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant had sexual intercourse with another person without their consent.

title: Third degree sexual assault: Sexual contact without consent involving ejaculation, etc.
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant had sexual contact with another person in the manner described in sub. (5)(b)2 or (5)(b)3 without the person’s consent.

title: Fourth degree sexual assault: sexual contact without consent
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant had sexual contact with another person without that person’s consent.

title: First degree reckless injury
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant recklessly caused great bodily harm to another human being under circumstances demonstrating utter disregard for human life.

title: Second degree reckless injury
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant recklessly caused great bodily harm to another human being or an unborn child.

title: Strangulation and suffocation
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant intentionally impeded the normal breathing or circulation of blood of another person by applying pressure on the throat or neck or by blocking the nose or mouth.

title: Injury by negligent handling of a dangerous weapon, explosives or fire.
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant caused bodily harm to another person through the negligent operation or handling of a dangerous weapon, explosives, or fire.
elements: Involvement of a Dangerous Weapon, Explosives, or Fire

title: Injury (great bodily harm) by operation of a vehicle while under the influence
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant caused great bodily harm to another human being by operating a vehicle while under the influence of an intoxicant.
elements: Under the Influence of an Intoxicant

title: Injury (great bodily harm) by operation of a vehicle while the person has a detectable amount of a restricted controlled substance influence
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant caused great bodily harm to another human being by operating a vehicle while having a detectable amount of a restricted controlled substance in their blood.
elements: Detectable Amount of a Restricted Controlled Substance

title: Injury (great bodily harm) by operation of a vehicle with a prohibited alcohol concentration
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant caused great bodily harm to another human being by operating a vehicle while having a prohibited alcohol concentration as defined in s. 340.01(46m).

title: Abuse of individuals at risk
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant subjected an individual at risk to abuse, either intentionally, recklessly, or negligently. This statute applies to individuals who are not in charge of or employed by certain facilities listed in s. 940.29 or s. 940.295(2).
elements: Death, Great Bodily Harm, or Bodily Harm

title: Abuse of residents of penal facilities
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant, who was in charge of or employed by a penal or correctional institution, abused, neglected, or ill-treated a person confined in or residing at such a facility, or knowingly allowed another person to do so.

title: Law enforcement officer - failure to render aid
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that a peace officer, while acting in the course of their employment or under the authority of their employment, intentionally failed to provide or arrange necessary first aid to a person in their custody, or knowingly allowed another person to do so, and that bodily harm resulted from the failure.
elements: Defendant’s Role as a Peace Officer
Failure to Render or Arrange First Aid
Failure to Render or Arrange First Aid

title: Abuse of patients and residents
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that a person in charge of or employed in a facility or program listed under sub. (2) intentionally or recklessly abused a patient or resident, or knowingly permitted another person to do so.

title: Neglect of patients and residents
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that a person in charge of or employed in a facility or program listed under sub. (2) intentionally or recklessly neglected a patient or resident, or knowingly permitted another person to do so.

title: False imprisonment
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant intentionally confined or restrained another person without their consent, knowing they had no lawful authority to do so.

title: Human trafficking
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant knowingly engaged in trafficking for either labor or services, or for a commercial sex act, using specific methods of coercion, threat, or control.

title: Human trafficking
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant knowingly received compensation derived from debt bondage, a prostitute, or a commercial sex act as described in sub. (1)(a)1 and 2.

title: Taking a hostage
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant seized, confined, or restrained a person without their consent, using force or the threat of imminent force, with the intent to use the person as a hostage to influence someone to perform or not perform a demanded action.
elements: Use of Force or Threat of Imminent Force
Intent to Use as a Hostage

title: Kidnapping
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant used force or the threat of imminent force to carry a person from one place to another without their consent, with the intent to secretly confine or imprison them, carry them out of the state, or hold them to service against their will.
elements: Force or Threat of Imminent Force

title: Kidnapping
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant, by force or threat of imminent force, seized or confined another person without their consent, with the intent to secretly confine, imprison, or carry them out of the state or hold them to service against their will.
elements: Force or Threat of Imminent Force

title: Kidnapping
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant, by deceit, induced another person to go from one place to another with the intent to secretly confine, imprison, or carry them out of the state, or hold them to service against their will.

title: Placing a global positioning device
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant placed a global positioning device or a device equipped with GPS technology on a vehicle owned or leased by another person without that person’s consent.

title: Obtaining information generated by a global positioning device
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant intentionally obtained information about another person’s movements or location from a global positioning device or device equipped with GPS technology that was placed without the other person’s consent.

title: Stalking
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant intentionally engaged in a course of conduct directed at a specific person using a global positioning device or similar technology, knowing that the conduct would cause serious emotional distress or fear of bodily injury or death to the victim or their family/household members.

title: Stalking
definition: To be guilty of this offense, the prosecution must prove that the defendant, after being convicted of sexual assault or a domestic abuse offense, engaged in certain prohibited conduct directed at the victim of the prior offense, knowing that the conduct would cause serious emotional distress or fear of bodily injury or death to the victim or their family/household members.
